## This study

this study argues that implementing a private social services architecture has consequences for the population’s normative judgments, with meritocracy emerging as a driving force shaping people’s conceptions of justice in the educational sphere. Meritocracy has been used as a narrative to define success and failure in terms of individual responsibility, especially in educational institutions where meritocracy plays a central role, so considering that, further argue that meritocratic beliefs provide a key normative lens through which individuals evaluate education inequalities. Based on this argument, this study aims to further explore the research area of market justice and meritocracy through two innovations: First, the identification of different belief systems in Chile using a multidimensional framework of meritocracy, distinguishing the heterogeneity of beliefs in terms of the size and number of recognizable systems. Second, to explore how each meritocratic belief system relates to preferences for market justice preferences in education. Thus, this study aims to demonstrate that meritocracy can function differently as a mechanism for legitimizing inequalities in education, and that this difference in its functioning as a mechanism can only be observed by acknowledging the heterogeneity of beliefs within the population. 

In light of the foregoing, it is worth analyzing this phenomenon in Chile, a country that offers an interesting case for examining how public attitudes toward the distribution of social services are affected by market-oriented welfare institutions. Chile is one of the most unequal countries in the OECD, with a high concentration of income and wealth in the top decile [@chancel_world_2026; @flores_top_2020]. This inequality is largely attributable to the neoliberal reforms of the civil-military dictatorship, subsequently expanded by democratic governments, which privatized and commodified key spheres of social reproduction through concessions and regulatory frameworks favorable to private provision [@madariaga_three_2020; @pnud_desiguales_2017]. This model has produced structurally segmented systems in health care, education, and pensions, where access and quality depend on the ability to pay, benefiting higher-income sectors and relegating the poorest to limited, underfunded public alternatives [@castillo_perceptions_2025; @boccardo_30_2020]. In detail, the education system is characterized as one of the most privatized in the world, where the quality of private education surpasses that of public education due to the limited regulation of the education market, and where high levels of private-sector investment coexist with a lack of public funding [@ramos_educacion_2022; @bellei_problema_2025; @valenzuela_socioeconomic_2014]. Thus, in a context marked by high and durable inequalities, a well-established education market, and the entrenchment of meritocratic beliefs, it becomes relevant to examine the link between meritocratic beliefs and preferences for education market justice [@castillo_perceptions_2025]. Ultimately, this research aims to explain how market-based normative beliefs may prevent educational institutions from ensuring equal opportunities, thereby bringing educational justice to the forefront of public discussion.
